questions.text: What is Henry's law ? Give one application of it.

answer.text:
Henry's law: the partial pressure of a gas above a solution is directly proportional to the mole fraction of the gas dissolved in the solution, i.e. $p = K_H\,x$, where $p$ = partial pressure of the gas, $x$ = its mole fraction in solution and $K_H$ = Henry's law constant.
Application (any one): to increase the solubility of $CO_2$ in soft drinks and soda water, the bottle is sealed under high pressure.

questions.text: The vapour pressure of pure liquid X and pure liquid Y at 25 °C are 120 mm Hg and 160 mm Hg respectively. If equal moles of X and Y are mixed to form an ideal solution, calculate the vapour pressure of the solution.

answer.text:
For an ideal binary solution, $p_{Total} = p^\circ_X\chi_X + p^\circ_Y\chi_Y$, with $\chi_X = \chi_Y = 0.5$.
$p_{Total} = (120 \times 0.5) + (160 \times 0.5) = 140\ \text{mm Hg}$.

questions.text: When $19{\cdot}5$ g of $F{-}CH_2{-}COOH$ (Molar mass $= 78$ g mol$^{-1}$), is dissolved in 500 g of water, the depression in freezing point is observed to be 1 °C. Calculate the degree of dissociation of $F{-}CH_2{-}COOH$. [Given : $K_f$ for water $= 1{\cdot}86$ K kg mol$^{-1}$]

answer.text:
$\Delta T_f = i\,K_f\,m = i\,K_f\,\dfrac{w_B}{M_B}\times\dfrac{1000}{w_A}$
$1 = i \times 1.86 \times \dfrac{19.5}{78}\times\dfrac{1000}{500}$, so $i = 1.075$.
Degree of dissociation $\alpha = \dfrac{i-1}{n-1} = \dfrac{1.075-1}{2-1} = 0.075$.

answer.text:

questions.text: $0{\cdot}3$ g of acetic acid (M $= 60$ g mol$^{-1}$) dissolved in 30 g of benzene shows a depression in freezing point equal to $0{\cdot}45$ °C. Calculate the percentage association of acid if it forms a dimer in the solution. [Given : $K_f$ for benzene $= 5{\cdot}12$ K kg mol$^{-1}$]

answer.text:
$\Delta T_f = i\,K_f\,\dfrac{w_B}{M_B}\times\dfrac{1000}{w_A}$
$0.45 = i \times 5.12 \times \dfrac{0.3}{60}\times\dfrac{1000}{30}$, so $i = 0.527$.
For association, $\alpha = \dfrac{1-i}{1-\frac{1}{n}} = \dfrac{1-0.527}{1-\frac{1}{2}} = 0.946$ (i.e. 94.6%).

questions.text: If benzoic acid (M $= 122$ g mol$^{-1}$) is associated into a dimer when dissolved in benzene and the osmotic pressure of a solution of $6{\cdot}1$ g of benzoic acid in 100 mL benzene is $6{\cdot}5$ atm at 27 °C, then what is the percentage association of benzoic acid ? (Given : R $= 0{\cdot}0821$ L atm K$^{-1}$ mol$^{-1}$)

answer.text:
$\pi = i\dfrac{n_B}{V}RT = i\dfrac{w_B}{M_B}\times\dfrac{1000}{V}\times RT$
$6.5 = i \times \dfrac{6.1}{122}\times\dfrac{1000}{100}\times 0.0821 \times 300$, so $i = \dfrac{6.5\times122}{6.1\times0.0821\times300\times10} = 0.528$.
For association, $\alpha = \dfrac{1-i}{1-\frac{1}{n}} = \dfrac{1-0.528}{1-\frac{1}{2}} = 0.944$ (i.e. 94.4%).

questions.text: (i) Why is boiling point of 1M NaCl solution more than that of 1M glucose solution ? (ii) A non-volatile solute 'X' (molar mass $= 50$ g mol$^{-1}$) when dissolved in 78 g of benzene reduced its vapour pressure to 90%. Calculate the mass of X dissolved in the solution. (iii) Calculate the boiling point elevation for a solution prepared by adding 10 g of $MgCl_2$ to 200 g of water assuming $MgCl_2$ is completely dissociated. ($K_b$ for Water $= 0{\cdot}512$ K kg mol$^{-1}$, Molar mass $MgCl_2 = 95$ g mol$^{-1}$)
questions.topic: Colligative Properties and Determination of Molar Mass

answer.text:
(a)(i) NaCl causes a greater colligative effect than glucose because NaCl dissociates, giving more particles in solution (its van't Hoff factor $i$ is greater than that of glucose).
(ii) Relative lowering of vapour pressure: $\dfrac{p^0 - p}{p^0} = x_2 = \dfrac{n_2}{n_1+n_2}$. With $p = 0.9\,p^0$ and $n_1 = \dfrac{78}{78} = 1$:
$\dfrac{p^0 - 0.9p^0}{p^0} = \dfrac{w/50}{(w/50)+1}$, giving $0.1\left(\dfrac{w}{50}+1\right) = \dfrac{w}{50}$, so $w = 5.55\ \text{g}$.
(iii) $\Delta T_b = i\,K_b\,m$ with $i = 3$: $\Delta T_b = 3 \times 0.512 \times \dfrac{10}{95}\times\dfrac{1000}{200} = 0.81\ \text{K (°C)}$.

questions.text: (i) Why is the value of Van't Hoff factor for ethanoic acid in benzene close to $0{\cdot}5$ ? (ii) Determine the osmotic pressure of a solution prepared by dissolving $2{\cdot}32 \times 10^{-2}$ g of $K_2SO_4$ in 2 L of solution at 25 °C, assuming $K_2SO_4$ is completely dissociated. (R $= 0{\cdot}082$ L atm K$^{-1}$ mol$^{-1}$, Molar mass $K_2SO_4 = 174$ g mol$^{-1}$) (iii) When $25{\cdot}6$ g of Sulphur was dissolved in 1000 g of benzene, the freezing point lowered by $0{\cdot}512$ K. Calculate the formula of Sulphur ($S_x$). ($K_f$ for benzene $= 5{\cdot}12$ K kg mol$^{-1}$, Atomic mass of Sulphur $= 32$ g mol$^{-1}$)

answer.text:
(b)(i) The van't Hoff factor of ethanoic acid (in benzene) is about $0.5$ because ethanoic-acid molecules associate to form dimers, so the number of particles is nearly halved.
(ii) $\pi = i\,CRT$ with $i = 3$: $\pi = 3 \times \dfrac{2.32\times10^{-2}}{174\times2}\times 0.082 \times 298 = 4.88\times10^{-3}\ \text{atm}$.
(iii) $\Delta T_b = K_f\,\dfrac{w_2}{M_2}\times\dfrac{1000}{w_1}$: $0.512 = 5.12 \times \dfrac{25.6}{M_2}\times\dfrac{1000}{1000}$, so $M_2 = 256$. Since $S \times x = 256$ and $S = 32$, $x = \dfrac{256}{32} = 8$, i.e. the molecular formula is $S_8$.

questions.text: The vapour pressure of a solvent at 283 K is 100 mm Hg. Calculate the vapour pressure of a dilute solution containing 1 mole of a strong electrolyte AB in 50 moles of the solvent at 283 K (assuming complete dissociation of solute AB).

answer.text:
AB is a strong electrolyte: AB → A⁺ + B⁻, so 1 mol AB gives i = 2 particles.
Particles of solute = 1 × 2 = 2 mol; solvent = 50 mol.
Mole fraction of solvent = 50/(50 + 2) = 50/52.
p(solution) = p°(solvent) × x(solvent) = 100 × 50/52 = 96.15 mm Hg.

questions.text: (i) State Kohlrausch's law of independent migration of ions. Write an expression for the limiting molar conductivity of acetic acid according to Kohlrausch's law. (ii) Calculate the maximum work and log $K_c$ for the given reaction at 298 K : $$Ni(s) + 2Ag^+(aq) \rightleftharpoons Ni^{2+}(aq) + 2Ag(s)$$ Given : $E^\circ_{Ni^{2+}/Ni} = -0{\cdot}25$ V, $E^\circ_{Ag^+/Ag} = +0{\cdot}80$ V, 1 F $= 96500$ C mol$^{-1}$.

answer.text:

$\Lambda_m^0(CH_3COOH) = \lambda^0_{CH_3COO^-} + \lambda^0_{H^+}$
(ii) $\Delta_rG^\circ = -nFE^\circ_{cell}$; maximum work $= -\Delta_rG^\circ = nFE^\circ_{cell}$
$= 2 \times 96500 \times (0.80 + 0.25) = 2 \times 96500 \times 1.05 = 202650\ \text{J mol}^{-1} \approx 202.65\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$.
$\log K_c = \dfrac{nE^\circ_{cell}}{0.059} = \dfrac{2 \times 1.05}{0.059} = 35.6$.

[$E^\circ_{cell} = +2{\cdot}71$ V, 1 F $= 96500$ C mol$^{-1}$, log 10 $= 1$]

answer.text:
(b)(i) Faraday's first law of electrolysis: the mass of a substance deposited or liberated at an electrode is directly proportional to the quantity of electricity (charge) passed through the electrolyte. (For $Mg^{2+} \to Mg$, 2 F of charge is required.)
(ii) Nernst equation for the cell:
$E_{cell} = E^\circ_{cell} - \dfrac{0.0591}{2}\log\dfrac{[Mg^{2+}]}{[Cu^{2+}]} = 2.71 - \dfrac{0.0591}{2}\log\dfrac{0.1}{0.01} = 2.71 - \dfrac{0.0591}{2}\log 10 = 2.71 - 0.0295 = 2.68\ \text{V}$.

(b) Calculate the $\Delta_rG^\circ$ and log $K_c$ for the given reaction at 298 K : $$Ni(s) + 2Ag^+(aq) \to Ni^{2+}(aq) + 2Ag(s)$$ Given : $E^\circ_{Ni^{2+}/Ni} = -0{\cdot}25$ V, $E^\circ_{Ag^+/Ag} = +0{\cdot}80$ V, 1F $= 96500$ C mol$^{-1}$.

answer.text:
(a) Molar conductivity $\Lambda_m = \dfrac{k}{c}\times 1000 = \dfrac{8\times10^{-5}}{2\times10^{-3}}\times 1000 = 40\ \text{S cm}^2\text{mol}^{-1}$.
Degree of dissociation $\alpha = \dfrac{\Lambda_m}{\Lambda_m^\circ} = \dfrac{40}{404} = 0.099$.
(b) $\Delta_rG^\circ = -nFE^\circ_{cell} = -2 \times 96500 \times (0.80+0.25) = -202650\ \text{J mol}^{-1} \approx -202.65\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$.
$\log K_c = \dfrac{nE^\circ_{cell}}{0.059} = \dfrac{2\times1.05}{0.059} = 35.6$.

questions.text: (a) Calculate the emf of the following cell at 25 °C : $Zn(s)\,|\,Zn^{2+}(0{\cdot}1\ M)\,\|\,H^+(0{\cdot}01\ M)\,|\,H_2(g)\,(1\ bar),\ Pt(s)$ [Given : $E^\circ_{Zn^{2+}/Zn} = -0{\cdot}76$ V, $E^\circ_{H^+/H_2} = 0{\cdot}00$ V, log 10 $= 1$] (b) State Kohlrausch law of independent migration of ions. Why does the conductivity of a solution decrease with dilution ?

answer.text:
(a) Nernst equation for the cell:
$E_{cell} = E^\circ_{cell} - \dfrac{0.059}{2}\log\dfrac{[Zn^{2+}]}{[H^+]^2} = 0.76 - \dfrac{0.059}{2}\log\dfrac{0.1}{(0.01)^2} = 0.76 - \dfrac{0.059}{2}\log 10^3 = 0.76 - \dfrac{0.059\times3}{2} = 0.671\ \text{V}$.
(b) Kohlrausch's law: the limiting molar conductivity of an electrolyte is equal to the sum of the individual contributions of its cation and anion. (On dilution the molar conductivity of a strong electrolyte increases only slightly because the number of ions per unit volume decreases.)

questions.text: (i) Calculate the emf of the following cell at 298 K : $Al(s)\,|\,Al^{3+}(0{\cdot}001\ M)\,\|\,Ni^{2+}(0{\cdot}1\ M)\,|\,Ni(s)$ [Given : $E^\circ_{Al^{3+}/Al} = -1{\cdot}66$ V, $E^\circ_{Ni^{2+}/Ni} = -0{\cdot}25$ V, log 10 $= 1$] (ii) With the help of a graph explain why it is not possible to determine $\Lambda^\circ_m$ for a weak electrolyte by extrapolating the molar conductivity ($\Lambda_m$) versus $C^{1/2}$ curve as for strong electrolyte.

answer.text:
(a) Nernst equation for the Al–Ni cell:
$E_{cell} = E^\circ_{cell} - \dfrac{0.059}{6}\log\dfrac{[Al^{3+}]^2}{[Ni^{2+}]^3} = [-0.25 + 1.66] - \dfrac{0.059}{6}\log\dfrac{(0.001)^2}{(0.1)^3} = 1.41 - \dfrac{0.059}{6}\log 10^{-3} = 1.41 + \dfrac{0.059\times3}{6} = 1.4395\ \text{V}$.
(b)(i) For a weak electrolyte, the plot of $\Lambda_m$ against $\sqrt{c}$ rises very steeply near $\sqrt{c}\to 0$ (the curve runs almost parallel to the $\Lambda_m$ axis).
(ii) Because the curve runs almost parallel to the y-axis, it does not intercept the axis even on extrapolation; hence $\Lambda_m^\circ$ of a weak electrolyte cannot be obtained by extrapolation.

questions.text: (i) The molar conductivities of $NH_4^+$ and $Cl^-$ ion are $73{\cdot}8$ S cm$^2$ mol$^{-1}$ and $76{\cdot}2$ S cm$^2$ mol$^{-1}$ respectively. The conductivity of $0{\cdot}1$ M $NH_4Cl$ is $1{\cdot}29 \times 10^{-2}$ S cm$^{-1}$. Calculate its molar conductivity and degree of dissociation. (ii) Calculate the half-cell potential at 298 K for the reaction $Zn^{2+} + 2e^- \longrightarrow Zn$ if $[Zn^{2+}] = 0{\cdot}1$ M and $E^\circ_{Zn^{2+}/Zn} = -0{\cdot}76$ V.

answer.text:
(i) $\Lambda_m^\circ(NH_4Cl) = \lambda^\circ_{NH_4^+} + \lambda^\circ_{Cl^-} = 73.8 + 76.2 = 150.0\ \text{S cm}^2\text{mol}^{-1}$.
$\Lambda_m = \dfrac{k}{c}\times1000 = \dfrac{1.29\times10^{-2}}{0.1}\times1000 = 129\ \text{S cm}^2\text{mol}^{-1}$.
$\alpha = \dfrac{\Lambda_m}{\Lambda_m^\circ} = \dfrac{129}{150} = 0.86$.
(ii) $E_{Zn^{2+}|Zn} = E^\circ_{Zn^{2+}|Zn} - \dfrac{0.059}{2}\log\dfrac{1}{[Zn^{2+}]} = -0.76 - \dfrac{0.059}{2}\log\dfrac{1}{0.1} = -0.76 - 0.0295 = -0.7895\ \text{V}$.

questions.text: Rahul set-up an experiment to find resistance of aqueous KCl solution for different concentrations at 298 K using a conductivity cell connected to a Wheatstone bridge. He fed the Wheatstone bridge with a.c. power in the audio frequency range 550 to 5000 cycles per second. Once the resistance was calculated from each half he also calculated the conductivity K and molar conductivity $\Lambda_m$ and recorded his readings in tabular form. Answer the following questions : (a) Why does conductivity decrease with dilution ? (b) If $\Lambda^\circ_m = 150{\cdot}0$ S cm$^2$ mol$^{-1}$, calculate the degree of dissociation of $0{\cdot}01$ M KCl. (c) If Rahul had used NaCl instead of KCl, would you expect the $\Lambda_m$ values to be more or less than those for KCl for a given concentration ? Justify. OR (c) Amit, a classmate of Rahul repeated the same experiment with $CH_3COOH$ solution instead of KCl solution. Give one point that would be similar and one that would be different in his observations as compared to Rahul.

answer.text:
(a) On dilution the molar conductivity increases because, although the number of ions per unit volume decreases, the ions move more freely (and for a weak electrolyte more of it dissociates).
(b) $\alpha = \dfrac{\Lambda_m}{\Lambda_m^\circ} = \dfrac{141}{150} = 0.94$.
(c) $H^+$ conducts more because the mobility of $H^+$ is greater than that of $K^+$.
OR (c) Similarity: for both electrolytes $\Lambda_m$ increases on dilution.
Difference: for KCl (a strong electrolyte) $\Lambda_m$ increases gradually and $\Lambda_m^\circ$ can be obtained by extrapolating $\Lambda_m$ to zero concentration; whereas for $CH_3COOH$ (a weak electrolyte) $\Lambda_m$ increases steeply on dilution and $\Lambda_m^\circ$ cannot be obtained by extrapolation.

questions.text: Calculate emf of the following cell at 25 °C : $Sn/Sn^{2+}(0{\cdot}001\ M)\,\|\,H^+(0{\cdot}01\ M)\,|\,H_{2(g)}(1\ bar)\,|\,Pt_{(s)}$. Given : $E^\circ(Sn^{2+}/Sn) = -0{\cdot}14$ V, $E^\circ(H^+/H_2) = 0{\cdot}00$ V (log 10 $= 1$)

In a galvanic cell, chemical energy of a redox reaction is converted into electrical energy, whereas in an electrolytic cell the redox reaction occurs on passing electricity. The simplest galvanic cell is one in which Zn rod is placed in a solution of $ZnSO_4$ and Cu rod is placed in a solution of $CuSO_4$. The two rods are connected by a metallic wire through a voltmeter. The two solutions are joined by a salt bridge. The difference between the two electrode potentials of the two electrodes is known as electromotive force. In the process of electrolysis, the decomposition of a substance takes place by passing an electric current. One mole of electric charge when passed through a cell will discharge half a mole of a divalent metal ion such as $Cu^{2+}$. This was first formulated by Faraday in the form of laws of electrolysis. Answer the following questions : (a) What is the function of a salt bridge in a galvanic cell ? (b) When does galvanic cell behave like an electrolytic cell ? (c) Can copper sulphate solution be stored in a pot made of zinc ? Explain with the help of the value of E° cell. ($E^\circ Cu^{2+}/Cu = 0{\cdot}34$ V) ($E^\circ Zn^{2+}/Zn = -0{\cdot}76$ V) OR (c) How much charge in terms of Faraday is required for the following : (i) 1 mol of $MnO_4^-$ to $Mn^{2+}$ (ii) 1 mol of $H_2O$ to $O_2$

answer.text:
(a) A salt bridge completes the circuit and maintains electrical neutrality of the two half-cells by allowing migration of ions, preventing accumulation of charge.
(b) A galvanic cell behaves like an electrolytic cell when an external opposing EMF greater than the cell's own EMF is applied, reversing the cell reaction.
(c) E°cell = E°(Cu²⁺/Cu) − E°(Zn²⁺/Zn) = 0.34 − (−0.76) = +1.10 V. Since E°cell is positive, Zn + Cu²⁺ → Zn²⁺ + Cu is spontaneous; so CuSO₄ CANNOT be stored in a zinc pot (zinc would displace copper and dissolve).
OR (c): (i) MnO₄⁻ → Mn²⁺ is a 5-electron reduction ⇒ 5 F. (ii) 2H₂O → O₂ + 4H⁺ + 4e⁻ ⇒ 4 F.

questions.text: A first order reaction is 50% complete in 30 minutes at 300 K and in 10 minutes at 320 K. Calculate activation energy ($E_a$) for the reaction. [R $= 8{\cdot}314$ J K$^{-1}$ mol$^{-1}$] [Given : log 2 $= 0{\cdot}3010$, log 3 $= 0{\cdot}4771$, log 4 $= 0{\cdot}6021$]

answer.text:
$k = \dfrac{0.693}{t_{1/2}}$, so $k_1 = \dfrac{0.693}{30}\ \text{min}^{-1}$ and $k_2 = \dfrac{0.693}{10}\ \text{min}^{-1}$.
$\log\dfrac{k_2}{k_1} = \dfrac{E_a}{2.303\,R}\left[\dfrac{1}{T_1} - \dfrac{1}{T_2}\right]$
$\log 3 = \dfrac{E_a}{2.303 \times 8.314}\left[\dfrac{1}{300} - \dfrac{1}{320}\right]$
$E_a = \dfrac{0.4771 \times 19.147 \times 300 \times 320}{20} = 43848\ \text{J mol}^{-1} \approx 43.85\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$.

questions.text: A chemical reaction $2N_2O_5(g) \longrightarrow 4NO_2(g) + O_2(g)$ in gas phase was carried out in a closed vessel. The concentration of $NO_2$ was found to increase by $5 \times 10^{-3}$ mol L$^{-1}$ in 10 seconds. Calculate : (a) the rate of formation of $NO_2$, and (b) the rate of consumption of $N_2O_5$.

answer.text:
For $2\,N_2O_5 \to 4\,NO_2 + O_2$:
$-\dfrac{1}{2}\dfrac{\Delta[N_2O_5]}{\Delta t} = \dfrac{1}{4}\dfrac{\Delta[NO_2]}{\Delta t} = \dfrac{\Delta[O_2]}{\Delta t}$
(a) Rate of formation of $NO_2$: $\dfrac{1}{4}\dfrac{\Delta[NO_2]}{\Delta t} = \dfrac{1}{4}\times\dfrac{5\times10^{-3}}{10} = 1.25\times10^{-4}\ \text{mol L}^{-1}\text{s}^{-1}$.
(b) Rate of disappearance of $N_2O_5$: $-\dfrac{\Delta[N_2O_5]}{\Delta t} = \dfrac{2}{4}\dfrac{\Delta[NO_2]}{\Delta t} = 0.5\times1.25\times10^{-4} = 0.625\times10^{-4} \ (= 6.25\times10^{-5})\ \text{mol L}^{-1}\text{s}^{-1}$.

questions.text: The rate of a reaction doubles when temperature changes from 27 °C to 37 °C. Calculate energy of activation for the reaction. (R $= 8{\cdot}314$ J K$^{-1}$ mol$^{-1}$) (Given : log 2 $= 0{\cdot}3010$, log 3 $= 0{\cdot}4771$, log 4 $= 0{\cdot}6021$)

answer.text:
When the rate constant doubles ($k_2 = 2k_1$) as T rises from 300 K to 310 K:
$\log\dfrac{k_2}{k_1} = \dfrac{E_a}{2.303\,R}\left[\dfrac{1}{T_1}-\dfrac{1}{T_2}\right]$
$\log 2 = \dfrac{E_a}{2.303\times8.314}\left[\dfrac{1}{300}-\dfrac{1}{310}\right]$
$E_a = \dfrac{0.3010\times19.147\times300\times310}{10} = 53598\ \text{J mol}^{-1} \approx 53.6\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$.

questions.text: In a reaction, the initial concentration of the reactants increases four fold and the rate becomes sixteen times its initial value. The order of the reaction is :

Rate constant for the first order decomposition of $N_2O_5$ is given by the following equation : $\log k = 23{\cdot}6 - \dfrac{2 \times 10^4\ K}{T}$. Calculate $E_a$ for this reaction. [R $= 8{\cdot}314$ J K$^{-1}$ mol$^{-1}$]

answer.text:
From the Arrhenius equation $\log k = \log A - \dfrac{E_a}{2.303\,RT}$, the slope of $\log k$ vs $1/T$ is $-\dfrac{E_a}{2.303\,R} = -2\times10^4\ \text{K}$.
$E_a = 2.303 \times 8.314\ \text{J K}^{-1}\text{mol}^{-1} \times 2\times10^4\ \text{K} = 3.830\times10^5\ \text{J mol}^{-1}$.

For the first-order gas-phase reaction, $k = \dfrac{2.303}{t}\log\dfrac{p_i}{2p_i - p_t}$

(a) Rate of reaction $= -\dfrac{1}{2}\dfrac{\Delta[N_2O_5]}{\Delta t} = \dfrac{1}{2}\times 1.4\times10^{-3} = 0.7\times10^{-3}\ \text{M s}^{-1}$ (i.e. $7\times10^{-4}\ \text{M s}^{-1}$).

questions.text: The rate of a chemical reaction is expressed either in terms of decrease in the concentration of reactants or increase in the concentration of a product per unit time. Rate of the reaction depends upon the nature of reactants, concentration of reactants, temperature, presence of catalyst, surface area of the reactants and presence of light. Rate of reaction is directly related to the concentration of reactant. Rate law states that the rate of reaction depends upon the concentration terms on which the rate of reaction actually depends, as observed experimentally. The sum of powers of the concentration of the reactants in the Rate law expression is called order of reaction while the number of reacting species taking part in an elementary reaction which must collide simultaneously in order to bring about a chemical reaction is called molecularity of the reaction. (a) (i) Slowest step.
(ii) Series of elementary reactions / Reactions involving two or more steps.
(b) Increases with increase in temperature.

questions.text: Assign reason for each of the following : (i) Manganese exhibits the highest oxidation state of $+7$ among the 3d series of transition elements. (ii) Transition metals and their compounds are generally found to be good catalysts in chemical reactions. (iii) $Cr^{2+}$ is reducing in nature while with the same d-orbital configuration ($d^4$) $Mn^{3+}$ is an oxidising agent. (iv) Zn has lowest enthalpy of atomization. (v) $Cu^+$ is unstable in an aqueous solution.
questions.topic: Electronic Configurations of the d-Block Elements

answer.text:
(i) Transition metals have high enthalpies of atomisation due to the participation of all the 3d and 4s electrons in interatomic (metallic) bonding / the presence of a large number of unpaired electrons.
(ii) They (and their compounds) act as good catalysts due to their variable oxidation states / ability to adopt multiple oxidation states / large surface area / complex formation.
(iii) $Cr^{2+}$ is a reducing agent because $Cr^{2+}\,(d^4) \to Cr^{3+}$ attains the stable half-filled $t_{2g}^3$ configuration, whereas $Mn^{3+}$ is an oxidising agent because $Mn^{3+} \to Mn^{2+}\,(d^5)$ attains the stable half-filled $d^5$ configuration.
(iv) (Zn, Cd and Hg have low melting points) due to the absence of unpaired d-electrons and hence weak interatomic interactions.
(v) $Cu^+$ ion (aq.) undergoes disproportionation to $Cu^{2+}$ (aq.) and Cu:
$2\,Cu^+(aq) \longrightarrow Cu^{2+}(aq) + Cu(s)$.

(ii) $Sc^{3+}$ is colourless whereas $Ti^{3+}$ is coloured in an aqueous solution. (iii) Actinoids show wide range of oxidation states. (ii) $Sc^{3+}$ is colourless because it has no unpaired electron in the d-orbital, whereas $Ti^{3+}$ has one unpaired electron and shows d–d transition (hence it is coloured).
(iii) Actinoids show a large number of oxidation states because of the comparable energies of the 5f, 6d and 7s orbitals.

questions.text: Which of the following is the most stable complex species ?

Coordination compounds are widely present in the minerals, plant and animal worlds and are known to play many important functions in the area of analytical chemistry, metallurgy, biological systems and medicine. Alfred Werner's theory postulated the use of two types of linkages (primary and secondary), by a metal atom/ion in a coordination compound. He predicted the geometrical shapes of a large number of coordination entities using the property of isomerism. The Valence Bond Theory (VBT) explains the formation, magnetic behaviour and geometrical shapes of coordination compounds. It, however, fails to describe the optical properties of these compounds. The Crystal Field Theory (CFT) explains the effect of different crystal fields (provided by the ligands taken as point charges) on the degeneracy of d-orbital energies of the central metal atom/ion. Answer the following questions : (i) When a coordination compound $NiCl_2 \cdot 6H_2O$ is mixed with $AgNO_3$ solution, 2 moles of AgCl are precipitated per mole of the compound. Write the structural formula of the complex and secondary valency for Nickel ion. (ii) Write the IUPAC name of the ionisation isomer of $[Co(NH_3)_5(SO_4)]Cl$. (iii) Using Valence Bond Theory, predict the geometry and magnetic nature of : (1) $[Ni(CO)_4]$ (2) $[Fe(CN)_6]^{3-}$ [Atomic number : Ni $= 28$, Fe $= 26$] OR (iii) Give reasons : (1) Low spin tetrahedral complexes are not formed. (2) $[Co(NH_3)_6]^{3+}$ is an inner orbital complex whereas $[Ni(NH_3)_6]^{2+}$ is an outer orbital complex. [Atomic number : Co $= 27$, Ni $= 28$]

answer.text:
(i) $[Ni(H_2O)_6]Cl_2$; coordination number = 6.
(ii) Pentaamminechloridocobalt(III) sulphate.
(iii)(1) $[Ni(CO)_4]$ — tetrahedral, diamagnetic. (2) $[Fe(CN)_6]^{3-}$ — octahedral, paramagnetic.
OR (iii)(1) In $[NiCl_4]^{2-}$, $\Delta_t$ (the crystal-field splitting energy, CFSE) is not sufficient to pair the electrons.
(2) $NH_3$, being a strong-field ligand, can pair up the electrons to form $d^2sp^3$; but in $Ni^{2+}$ two vacant (inner) d-orbitals are not available, so $sp^3d^2$ is formed instead.

questions.text: Answer any three of the following questions : (a) Explain the type of hybridization in $[Fe(CN)_6]^{3-}$ on the basis of valence bond theory. (Given : Atomic number of Fe $= 26$) (b) Draw the geometrical isomers of $[PtCl_2(en)_2]^{2+}$ ion. (c) $[NiCl_4]^{2-}$ is paramagnetic while $[Ni(CO)_4]$ is diamagnetic though both are tetrahedral. Why ? (d) Name the type of isomerism when ambidentate ligands are attached to central metal ion. Give one example of ambidentate ligand.

answer.text:
(a) $Fe = 3d^6 4s^2$, so $Fe^{3+} = 3d^5$. In $[Fe(CN)_6]^{3-}$, $CN^-$ (a strong-field ligand) pairs the d-electrons, leaving two inner d-orbitals vacant; hence the hybridisation is $d^2sp^3$ (octahedral).
(b) $[Pt(en)_2Cl_2]^{2+}$ shows cis–trans (geometrical) isomerism: in the cis isomer the two $Cl$ ligands are adjacent, and in the trans isomer they are opposite.
(c) $Cl^-$, being a weak-field ligand, does not cause pairing, so $[NiCl_4]^{2-}$ is paramagnetic; whereas CO, being a strong-field ligand, causes pairing, so $[Ni(CO)_4]$ is diamagnetic.
(d) Linkage isomerism. Example: ambidentate ligands such as $CN^-$ / $NO_2^-$ / $SCN^-$.

questions.text: The polarity of C $-$ X bond of alkyl halides is responsible for their nucleophilic substitution, elimination and their reaction with metal atoms to form organometallic compounds. Aryl halides are prepared by electrophilic substitution of arenes. Nucleophilic substitution reactions are categorised into $S_N^1$ and $S_N^2$ on the basis of their kinetic properties. answer.text:
(i) $C_6H_5MgBr$ (phenylmagnesium bromide) is formed.

questions.text: Nucleophilic Substitution reaction of haloalkane can be conducted according to both $S_N1$ and $S_N2$ mechanisms. $S_N1$ is a two step reaction while $S_N2$ is a single step reaction. For any haloalkane which mechanism is followed depends on factors such as structure of haloalkane, properties of leaving group, nucleophilic reagent and solvent. In $S_N1$ reaction, the polarity of the system increases from the reactant to the transition state, because a polar solvent has a greater effect on the transition state than the reactant, thereby reducing activation energy and accelerating the reaction. In $S_N2$ reaction, the polarity of the system generally does not change from the reactant to the transition state and only charge dispersion occurs. Generally weak polar solvent is favourable for $S_N2$ reaction, while strong polar solvent is favourable for $S_N1$. Answer the following questions : (a) Why racemisation occurs in $S_N1$ ? (b) Why is ethanol less polar than water ? (c) Which one of the following in each pair is more reactive towards $S_N2$ reaction ? answer.text:
(a) A tertiary halide undergoes $S_N1$ readily because of the formation of a stable planar ($sp^2$-hybridised) carbocation.
(b) Ethanol is a weaker acid than water due to the +I effect (electron-releasing nature) of the ethyl group.
(c)(i) $CH_3CH_2I$ (iodoethane).
(ii) Benzyl chloride, $C_6H_5{-}CH_2{-}Cl$.
OR (c)(i) Increasing order of reactivity towards $S_N1$: 1-bromopentane < 2-bromopentane < 2-bromo-2-methylbutane.
(ii) Increasing order of reactivity towards $S_N1$: 1-bromo-3-methylbutane < 2-bromo-3-methylbutane < 2-bromo-2-methylbutane.

questions.text: (i) Write the mechanism of the following reaction : $CH_3CH_2OH \xrightarrow[\;443\ K\;]{\;H^+\;} CH_2{=}CH_2 + H_2O$ (ii) Write the equation involved in Reimer-Tiemann reaction.

questions.text: (i) Write the mechanism of the following reaction : $2CH_3CH_2OH \xrightarrow[\;413\ K\;]{\;H^+\;} CH_3{-}CH_2{-}O{-}CH_2{-}CH_3 + H_2O$ (ii) Why ortho-nitrophenol is steam volatile while para-nitrophenol is not ?

answer.text:
(a)(i) Acid-catalysed formation of diethyl ether from ethanol (mechanism): ethanol is first protonated by $H^+$; a second ethanol molecule then attacks the protonated ethanol (nucleophilic substitution), losing water to give protonated diethyl ether, which loses a proton to give diethyl ether:
$C_2H_5OH + H^+ \rightarrow C_2H_5\overset{+}{O}H_2$; then $C_2H_5OH + C_2H_5\overset{+}{O}H_2 \rightarrow C_2H_5{-}\overset{+}{O}H{-}C_2H_5 + H_2O \rightarrow C_2H_5{-}O{-}C_2H_5 + H^+$.
(ii) o-Nitrophenol is steam-volatile (more volatile than p-nitrophenol) because o-nitrophenol has intramolecular H-bonding, whereas p-nitrophenol has intermolecular H-bonding.

questions.text: (a) Write the mechanism of the following reaction : $CH_3{-}CH_2{-}OH \xrightarrow[\;443\ K\;]{\;H^+\;} CH_2{=}CH_2 + H_2O$ (b) Write the equation of the reaction for the preparation of phenol from cumene.

answer.text:
(a) Acid-catalysed dehydration of ethanol to ethene (mechanism): ethanol is protonated (fast) to the oxonium ion, which loses water (slow) to form the ethyl carbocation, which then loses a proton to give ethene:
$C_2H_5OH + H^+ \rightleftharpoons C_2H_5\overset{+}{O}H_2 \rightleftharpoons CH_3\overset{+}{C}H_2 + H_2O \rightleftharpoons CH_2{=}CH_2 + H^+$.

questions.text: Explain the mechanism of acid catalysed hydration of ethene.

answer.text:
Acid-catalysed hydration of ethene (mechanism):
Step 1 — Protonation of the alkene: CH₂=CH₂ + H⁺ → CH₃–CH₂⁺ (carbocation).
Step 2 — Nucleophilic attack of water on the carbocation: CH₃–CH₂⁺ + H₂O → CH₃–CH₂–OH₂⁺.
Step 3 — Loss of a proton: CH₃–CH₂–OH₂⁺ → CH₃–CH₂–OH + H⁺ (catalyst regenerated).

OR (c)(i) The compound is 3-oxocyclohexane-1-carboxylate (a cyclohexanone ring bearing a $-COO^-$ group).
(ii) The compound is the semicarbazone of benzaldehyde ($C_6H_5{-}CH{=}N{-}NH{-}CO{-}NH_2$).

(b) Which acid of the following pair is a stronger acid ? $F_3C{-}C_6H_4{-}COOH$ or $H_3C{-}C_6H_4{-}COOH$ (c) Write the chemical equation involved in Rosenmund's reduction. (d) Why are $\alpha$-hydrogen atoms of aldehydes and ketones acidic in nature ? (e) Write a chemical test to distinguish between Benzaldehyde and Benzoic acid.

answer.text:
(a) The product is the 2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazone of benzaldehyde: $C_6H_5{-}CH{=}N{-}NH{-}C_6H_3(NO_2)_2$.
(b) The strongest acid is 4-(trifluoromethyl)benzoic acid, $F_3C{-}C_6H_4{-}COOH$ (the $-CF_3$ group is strongly electron-withdrawing).
(c) Rosenmund reduction: $C_6H_5COCl \xrightarrow{H_2,\ Pd{-}BaSO_4} C_6H_5CHO$ (benzaldehyde).
(d) Due to the resonance stabilisation of the conjugate base (the enolate ion) — which makes the $\alpha$-hydrogen acidic.

questions.text: (i) Write the reaction involved in Cannizzaro's reaction. (ii) Why is the boiling point of aldehydes and ketones lower than that of corresponding carboxylic acids ? (iii) An organic compound 'A' with molecular formula $C_5H_8O_2$ is reduced to n-pentane with hydrazine followed by heating with NaOH and Glycol. 'A' forms a dioxime with hydroxylamine and gives a positive Iodoform and Tollen's test. Identify 'A' and give its reaction for Iodoform and Tollen's test.

answer.text:
(a)(i) Cannizzaro reaction of methanal (formaldehyde) with conc. KOH gives methanol and potassium formate:
$2\,HCHO \xrightarrow[\Delta]{\text{conc. }KOH} CH_3OH + HCOOK$.
(ii) Carboxylic acids have higher boiling points than aldehydes/ketones because they have strong intermolecular hydrogen bonding, whereas aldehydes and ketones have only weak dipole–dipole interactions.
(iii) $A = $ 4-oxopentanal, $CH_3{-}CO{-}CH_2{-}CH_2{-}CHO$.
It gives a positive iodoform test (yellow ppt of $CHI_3$) with $NaOH + I_2$ (due to the $CH_3CO-$ group), and its $-CHO$ group is oxidised by Tollens' reagent to the carboxylate with a silver mirror:
$CH_3CO{-}CH_2CH_2{-}CHO \xrightarrow[\text{warm}]{[Ag(NH_3)_2]^+,\ OH^-} CH_3CO{-}CH_2{-}CH_2{-}COO^- + Ag\downarrow$.

questions.text: (I) Give reasons : (i) Aniline on nitration gives good amount of m-nitroaniline, though $-NH_2$ group is o/p directing in electrophilic substitution reactions. questions.text: Amines are usually formed from nitro compounds, halides, amides, imides, etc. They exhibit hydrogen bonding which influences their physical properties. In alkyl amines, a combination of electron releasing, steric and hydrogen bonding factors influence the stability of the substituted ammonium cations in protic polar solvents and thus affect the basic nature of amines. In aromatic amines, electron releasing and withdrawing groups, respectively increase and decrease their basic character. Influence of the number of hydrogen atoms at nitrogen atom on the type of reactions and nature of products is responsible for identification and distinction between primary, secondary and tertiary amines. questions.text: Living systems are made up of various complex biomolecules like carbohydrates, proteins, nucleic acids, lipids, etc. Carbohydrates are optically active polyhydroxy aldehydes or ketones or molecules which provide such units on hydrolysis. They are broadly classified into three groups — monosaccharides, oligosaccharides and polysaccharides. Monosaccharides are held together by glycosidic linkages to form disaccharides like sucrose, maltose or polysaccharides like starch and cellulose. Another biomolecule : proteins are polymers of $\alpha$-amino acids which are linked by peptide bonds. Ten amino acids are called essential amino acids. (iii) What are the common types of secondary structures of proteins ? Write any two forces which stabilise the secondary and tertiary structures of protein. answer.text:
(i) Peptide linkage: the $-CO{-}NH-$ linkage formed when two amino acids are joined. Glycosidic linkage: the linkage formed when two monosaccharides are joined through an oxygen atom.
(ii) Essential amino acids: those which are not synthesised in the body and must be obtained through the diet.
(iii) The two secondary structures of proteins are the $\alpha$-helix and the $\beta$-pleated sheet; they are stabilised by (any two): hydrogen bonds, van der Waals forces, disulphide linkages, electrostatic forces of attraction.
OR (iii) Denaturation: the loss of biological activity when the native form of a protein is subjected to a change in temperature, pH, etc. (e.g. the curdling of milk). During denaturation the secondary and tertiary structures are lost, so the protein loses its biological activity.
